Perfect verb, Form I, 3rd person feminine plural. The -na suffix marks feminine plural subject, referring back to the feminine plural participles al-'adiyat/al-muriyat/al-mughirat. Transitive: takes naq'an as direct object.
Perfect verb, Form I, 3rd person feminine plural. Subject is the mares (al-'adiyat) from 100:1, carried across the oath. Transitive — takes jam'an as direct object.
Imperfect verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. Subject is the human (al-insan) from 100:6. Used here without explicit object — object is elided.
notes: object_not_surface

grammar: Passive perfect (PV_PASS) of the quadriliteral verb ba'thara. 3rd person masculine singular agreeing with the masculine default for ma (what). The perfect tense after idha indicates certainty of the future event.

Passive perfect verb (fi'l māḍī majhūl), Form II (fu''ila pattern). The Form II intensification of the root ḥ-ṣ-l adds thoroughness: not merely obtaining but thoroughly extracting, separating completely. Subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) is the following mā fī ṣ-ṣudūri. The agent is deliberately left unspecified by the passive construction.

Perfect verb, Form IV (af'ala), 3rd person masculine singular with 2nd person masculine singular object suffix -ka. Form IV is causative: "to cause someone to know/perceive." The subject is the preceding ma (what).

Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular, indicative (marfūʿ). Functions as a copula (IV_COP in MASAQ) linking the subject an-nāsu to the predicate ka-l-farāshi. The imperfect tense here denotes a future state (the Day has not yet come). yakūnu without an explicit predicate noun (khabar) uses the prepositional simile ka-l-farāsh as its predicate, creating an identity-transformation: "becomes as" rather than "resembles."
notes: كَ phrase is the copular predicate

grammar: Imperfect verb, Form I, 3rd person feminine singular (agreeing with al-jibalu, broken plural treated as feminine). Copulative (IV_COP) usage linking subject to predicate. The imperfect tense signals eschatological futurity.
notes: كَ phrase is the copular predicate

grammar: Form I past verb (fa'ula pattern — stative/qualitative); 3rd person feminine singular; the feminine marker -t agrees with the grammatical feminine of mawazin; fa'ula pattern indicates inherent quality rather than acquired action; intransitive (no direct object — the scales themselves are the subject)

Perfect (past) verb (fi'l māḍī), Form I (فَعَّ / fa''a with doubled final radical), 3rd person feminine singular. The feminine agreement is with mawāzīn (broken plural treated as feminine). The doubled fā' (فّ) is a geminate root pattern: kh-f-f, where the second and third radicals are identical. The perfect tense places the lightness as an accomplished fact — a realized state, not an ongoing process.

Perfect verb, Form IV (af'ala), 3rd person masculine singular with 2nd person masculine singular object suffix -ka. Form IV is causative: "to cause someone to know/perceive." Subject is the preceding interrogative ma.

Perfect verb, Form IV (af'ala), 3rd person masculine singular with 2nd person masculine plural object suffix -kum. Form IV is causative: "caused you to be diverted/amused." The alif-lam-ha-ya structure with the IV pattern indicates making someone else experience lahw.

Perfect verb, Form I, 2nd person masculine plural. The perfect tense here functions as a prophetic perfect (madi expressing future certainty) or a literal past narrating what has already occurred to previous generations.

Form I imperfect indicative, 2nd person masculine plural. From root ʿ-l-m. Used here WITHOUT a direct object (intransitive), though the verb is typically transitive (MIXED transitivity: 290 with object, 44 without in Quranic usage). The absence of object is deliberate rhetorical elision (ḥadhf al-mafʿūl) — the unspecified object becomes maximally inclusive.
notes: علم has no overt object here

grammar: Form I imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), 2nd person masculine plural. Used here intransitively — no direct object is stated; the object of knowledge is deliberately elided (ḥadhf al-mafʿūl bihi), creating semantic openness. The verb ʿalima in Form I fundamentally means "to know, to become aware, to perceive" and can take a direct object (transitive) or be used absolutely (intransitive). The ROOT DATA shows MIXED transitivity (290 with object, 44 without), and this ayah is listed among the without-object instances, confirming the intransitive reading. The same form taʿlamūna appears in 102:3 without thumma.
notes: علم has no overt object here

grammar: Form I imperfect (muḍāriʿ), 2nd person masculine plural. The verb here takes a cognate accusative (mafʿūl muṭlaq): ʿilma l-yaqīni. Mixed transitivity: 290 instances with explicit object vs. 44 without — here the cognate accusative serves as the object, making this a transitive usage. The imperfect after law is grammatically unusual (see CRITICAL for law).
notes: cognate accusative is not a direct object

grammar: Form IV imperfect (muḍāriʿ), 2nd person masculine plural. Suffixed with nūn at-tawkīd ath-thaqīla (نَّ, heavy energetic nūn). The original form would be tarawna → with energetic nūn → tarawunna. The wāw of the plural conjugation is retained before the nūn. Form IV (arā/yurī) is causative-transitive: "to make see, to show" — but in common usage it functions as the standard transitive "to see (something)." The verb takes al-jaḥīm as its direct object (mafʿūl bih).

Form IV imperfect verb, 2nd person masculine plural, with nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīla (heavy energetic nūn) suffix, plus attached object pronoun -hā (3fs, referring to al-jaḥīm from 102:6). Base: tarawna → with tawkīd: tarawunna → with -hā: tarawunnahā. Form IV (arā / yurī) of r-'-y in common usage functions identically to Form I for "seeing." The energetic nūn construction is among the strongest assertion forms in Arabic — it appears only after an oath (explicit or implied) and conveys absolute certainty of occurrence.

Form I passive imperfect (tus'alu) with heavy nūn al-tawkīd (-unna). Second person masculine plural. The passive voice (mabnī li-l-majhūl) removes the agent: WHO questions is unstated. The verb governs the prepositional phrase ʿan al-naʿīm (questioned ABOUT). MIXED transitivity: in 8 of 12 IV_PASS occurrences the verb appears without a direct object, relying on the ʿan-phrase to specify the topic.

Perfect verb (fi'l madi), Form IV (af'ala), 3rd person masculine plural. Form IV is causative/declarative: "to render oneself secure" or "to declare trust." The plural waw suffix refers back to alladhina. No explicit object — the verb is used absolutely (intransitively) here.
Perfect verb (fi'l madi), Form I (fa'ila), 3rd person masculine plural. Transitive here with direct object as-salihati. The plural waw suffix refers to alladhina.

Perfect verb (fi'l madi), Form VI (tafa'ala), 3rd person masculine plural. Form VI is reciprocal: the action is mutual — each person both gives and receives the charge. The base root w-s-y means to charge, bequeath, counsel, entrust with a final directive.
Perfect verb (fi'l madi), Form VI (tafa'ala), 3rd person masculine plural. Identical morphology to word 8. Second occurrence in the ayah, this time paired with bi-s-sabri instead of bi-l-haqqi.
Perfect verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. Transitive, taking malan as direct object (accusative). MIXED transitivity: 10 with object, 3 without.
Perfect verb, Form II (fa''ala pattern, with tashdid on dal), 3rd person masculine singular with 3rd person masculine singular object suffix -hu. TRANSITIVE: 34 with object, 0 without in PV form.

Form I imperfect indicative, 3rd person masculine singular. Active voice. Governs the anna-clause as its object. The imperfect tense signals habitual, ongoing action — this is not a single moment of thought but a persistent state of mind.

Form IV perfect verb, 3rd person masculine singular, with attached object pronoun -hū. Subject is mālahū (his wealth). Form IV (af'ala) is CAUSATIVE: "to cause someone to be khālid (permanent/immortal)." Perfect tense signals a completed action — in the subject's mind, the immortalization is already accomplished.

Passive imperfect verb, (Form I), 3rd person masculine singular, with nūn al-tawkīd al-thaqīla (heavy energetic nūn) suffix; passive voice — the subject IS thrown, not throws; the energetic nūn binds to the lām al-qasam at the prefix to produce a sworn future
Perfect verb, Form IV (af'ala — causative), 3rd person masculine singular with 2nd person masculine singular object suffix -ka. Form IV adds causative meaning: "to cause to know/perceive."
notes: أَدْرَى takes the addressed pronoun and embedded question

grammar: Form VIII (iftiʿāla: iṭṭalaʿa) imperfect, 3rd person feminine singular, indicative (marfūʿ). Subject is implicit (hiya, referring to al-ḥuṭama via allatī). The Form VIII pattern adds reflexive/intensive meaning to the base root: not merely "rising" (Form I ṭalaʿa) but "striving to rise, seeking to know, peering deliberately." The imperfect tense indicates ongoing, continuous action — the fire perpetually ascends/peers. MASAQ labels this as "IV" but the morphological pattern (ta-ṭṭ-aliʿ-u with assimilation of tāʾ of iftaʿala into ṭāʾ) is Form VIII. Transitivity: MIXED — the bundle shows 5 occurrences with object, 1 without (this ayah, 104:7). The objectless use here is significant: the fire peers INTO (ʿalā) hearts via preposition, not taking a direct accusative object. This intransitive-with-preposition construction shifts from "gaining knowledge OF something" to "rising/ascending UPON something."

Form IV (arā/yarā) imperfect 2ms in jussive mood (apocopated: tara < tarā); the IV form adds causative or intensive nuance — not merely "to see" but "to be made to see / to perceive deeply"; loss of final alif due to jazm by lam

Perfect (past) verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular; subject is rabbuka (your Lord); used here WITHOUT explicit direct object — the action's content is deliberately unstated, to be elaborated in subsequent ayahs

Imperfect verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular, jussive mood (apocopated by lam). ja'ala is a double-accusative or accusative + prepositional complement verb: ja'ala X fi Y = "he placed/rendered X in(to) Y."

Perfect verb, Form IV (af'ala), 3rd person masculine singular. Subject (God/rabbuka) elided, carried from 105:1. Takes direct object (tayran) and prepositional complement ('alayhim). Form IV adds causative meaning: "caused to be sent/dispatched."

Imperfect verb (muḍāri'), 3rd person feminine singular, Form I. The feminine gender agrees with ṭayr (birds, grammatically feminine collective) from 105:3. The suffix -him is 3rd person masculine plural object pronoun referring to aṣḥāb al-fīl (the elephant people). MIXED transitivity: the verb can take a direct object (ramā fulānan) or use bi- for the projectile (ramā bi-shay'in).

Perfect verb (fa'ala, Form I), 3rd person masculine singular with 3rd person masculine plural object suffix -hum. Double accusative construction: first object -hum (them), second object/predicate ka-'aṣfin ma'kūlin (like eaten straw). The subject is God (implied from the surah context).

Jussive imperfect verb (muḍāri' majzūm) governed by lām al-amr. Third person masculine plural. Form I (fa'ala). The wāw is the plural subject marker. The original form ya'budūna loses its final nūn due to jazm (apocopation by lām al-amr). Direct object: rabba (accusative).

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form IV (afʿala), 3rd person masculine singular + 3rd person masculine plural object suffix (-hum). Form IV is causative: "He caused them to taste/eat." The root ṭ-ʿ-m in Form I means "to taste, to eat"; Form IV shifts to "to cause to taste, to feed, to nourish." The -hum suffix refers to the Quraysh.

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form IV (afʿala), 3rd person masculine singular + 3rd person masculine plural object suffix (-hum). Form IV of '-m-n is causative: "He caused them to be safe / He granted them security." In Form I, amina means "to be safe, to trust"; Form IV shifts to "to make safe, to secure, to grant amān (safety/protection)." The -hum suffix refers to the Quraysh.

Perfect verb, Form I, 2nd person masculine singular, with interrogative hamza prefix (أ). Root r-'-y yields ra'a (to see). The perfect tense indicates completed/established recognition. Interrogative hamza transforms a declarative into a question, but in Quranic usage ara'ayta often functions as a rhetorical device: "Consider!" or "Have you noticed!"

Imperfect verb, Form II (fa''ala pattern), 3rd person masculine singular. Form II of k-dh-b intensifies the basic meaning: not merely "to lie" but "to actively deny, to declare false, to treat as a lie." The imperfect indicates ongoing, habitual action — this person continuously denies.
notes: argument expressed through بـ complement

grammar: Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular, active voice, indicative mood (marfūʿ). From the geminate/doubled root د ع ع (d-ʿ-ʿ) — NOT the common root د ع و (d-ʿ-w, "to call/invoke"). The doubling of the final radical (shadda on ʿayn) is the morphological marker: daʿʿa/yaduʿʿu = to push, repulse, shove. The imperfect tense marks HABITUAL action — this is something the person does repeatedly, not once. Direct object: al-yatīma (the orphan) in the accusative.

Form IV imperfect verb (yufa''ilu pattern), 3rd person masculine singular. The doubled final radical (ḍ-ḍ) creates the intensive phonetic quality. Used here without an explicit direct object — the person/entity being urged is elided. Governs the prepositional phrase ʿalā ṭaʿāmi l-miskīni. Transitivity flag: MIXED (1 with object, 3 without in Quran). In 107:3 the verb is objectless, matching the dominant Quranic pattern.
notes: urged person not expressed

grammar: Form III imperfect verb (yufāʿilūna pattern), 3rd person masculine plural, indicative (marfūʿ). From r-ʾ-y (to see), Form III rāʾā / yurāʾī means "to show, to display, to make visible to others, to do something to be seen." The MASAQ tags this as IV, but morphologically yurāʾūna follows the yufāʿilu pattern of Form III (مُفَاعَلَة), not the yufiʿlu pattern of Form IV. Form III adds the dimension of mutual/reciprocal action: showing AND seeking to be seen. The verb has no explicit object — what they show or whom they show to is deliberately unspecified, creating universal scope: they perform ANY act for the sake of being seen. The derived noun riyāʾ (ostentation, showing off) comes from this same form. Transitivity: the verb appears WITHOUT an explicit direct object (listed among without_object_ayahs in ROOT DATA: 107:6), meaning the showing is absolute/intransitive — they "do showing" rather than "show something specific."

Imperfect (mudari') verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine plural, active voice, indicative mood (marfu'). Subject is the implicit "they" referring to the hypocritical worshippers described in 107:4-6. Governs al-ma'una as direct object in the accusative.

Perfect verb (PV), Form IV (af'ala), 1st person plural subject + 2nd person masculine singular object suffix -ka. Form IV is causative: "to cause to have, to grant." Double transitive: takes both a person (you) and a thing (al-kawthar) as objects.

Form II imperative (فَعِّلْ / faʿʿil) — 2nd person masculine singular, apocopated (مجزوم / majzūm). The tashkīl (شدّة / shadda on the lām) confirms Form II (intensive/causative). MIXED transitivity: appears with object (عَلَيْهِمْ in 9:103, عَلَيْهِ in 33:56) and without object (33:56 صَلُّوا, 108:2). Here used without direct object — the لِرَبِّكَ phrase provides directional complement, not a direct object.

Form I imperative (اِفْعَلْ / ifʿal) — 2nd person masculine singular, apocopated (مجزوم / majzūm). The hamzat al-waṣl (ٱ) indicates the imperative of a triliteral verb with initial sukūn cluster. INTRANSITIVE in this ayah (no stated object). The root ن ح ر appears ONLY HERE in the entire Quran — a hapax legomenon. This sole occurrence makes the word's meaning entirely dependent on classical lexicon evidence and the root's pre-Quranic/extra-Quranic semantic field.

Imperative (amr), 2nd person masculine singular, from Form I of q-w-l. The apocopated form (majzūm/mabni): the lām carries sukūn. No explicit object — the content of what to say follows as the entire surah. This is a "say"-command (qul) which occurs 332 times in the Quran, establishing the Prophet as transmitter rather than originator of the message. The verb is transitive; its object here is the entire quoted speech that follows (109:2-6).

Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I (fa'ala / yaf'ulu pattern), 1st person singular, indicative (marfūʿ — marked by ḍamma on the dāl). Active voice. The verb takes a direct object (mā taʿbudūna) — transitive usage. Negated by the preceding lā, creating "I do not worship." The Form I imperfect of ʿ-b-d follows the yaf'ulu pattern (medial 'ayn with ḍamma), indicating the sound/healthy verb paradigm.

Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I, 2nd person masculine plural, indicative (marfūʿ — marked by the nūn of rafʿ). Active voice. This is the same verb as aʿbudu (word 2) but in 2nd person plural — the grammatical person shift from "I" to "you (all)" within the same root is the engine of the ayah's meaning. Functions as the ṣila (relative clause verb) completing mā.

Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I (فَعَلَ), first person singular (anā), indicative mood (marfūʿ). Functions as the verb of the relative clause introduced by mā. The imperfect tense indicates ongoing, habitual action — "what I [habitually/continuously] worship," not "what I worshipped once." The first person singular contrasts with the second person plural of the main clause (antum), reinforcing the I/you binary.

Perfect/past verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form I (faʿala), second person masculine plural (antum). The tāʾ is the subject pronoun suffix (-tum, "you all"), and the doubling (تُّ, with shadda) is due to assimilation of the original dāl of عَبَد + تُمْ. Transitive: takes مَّا as its implicit object (the relative pronoun refers back to the object of worship). The past tense is significant — it describes worship that has already been established as historical fact.

Imperfect verb (mudari'), Form I, 1st person singular. The imperfect tense denotes ongoing, habitual, continuous action: "what I [continuously] worship." The absence of an explicit subject pronoun (ana) contrasts with the emphatic antum in the main clause — the speaker's identity is subsumed into the act of worship itself.

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), 3rd person masculine singular. Subject: naṣru llāhi wa-l-fatḥu (compound subject — the verb agrees with the first element, naṣr, which is masculine singular). The perfect tense after idhā expresses future certainty. Transitivity: MIXED — this verb can take a direct object (252 instances) or be used intransitively (24 instances). Here used intransitively: no explicit object, naṣr and al-fatḥ are subjects that "come/arrive."
notes: جَآءَ takes the arriving entity as subject.

grammar: Perfect verb (māḍī), Form I, 2nd person masculine singular. Root r-'-y. With explicit accusative object (an-nāsa) = transitive visual perception. The perfect tense frames this as accomplished fact. Can carry meanings of physical sight, cognitive realization, or experiential knowledge. Followed by ḥāl clause (yadkhulūna).

Imperfect verb (muḍāriʿ), Form I, 3rd person masculine plural. Root d-kh-l. Functions as ḥāl (circumstantial clause) describing the state of an-nāsa: "the people [in the state of] entering." The imperfect tense marks the action as ongoing/progressive/incomplete — they are in the process of entering, not finished entering. Syntactic role: IV (imperfect verb in ḥāl clause).

Form II imperative (fi'l amr, bāb al-taf'īl), 2nd person masculine singular. The base root s-b-h means "to swim, to glide, to move freely through a medium." Form II intensifies: "to declare repeatedly/intensely free from limitation" or "to move with sustained, purposeful gliding." The verb here is intransitive (no direct object) — glorification is performed bi-ḥamdi (through praise), making praise the instrument, not the object. Apocopated (majzūm) as imperative form.
notes: direct object absent while بِحَمْدِ supplies the expressed complement

grammar: Form X imperative (fi'l amr, bāb al-istif'āl), 2nd person masculine singular, with attached 3rd person masculine singular object pronoun -hu. Form X of gh-f-r: to seek (ista-) covering/forgiveness (ghafr). The -hu pronoun refers back to rabb. The verb is transitive here with an explicit object (the pronoun). Apocopated as imperative.

Past tense verb (fi'l māḍī), 3rd person masculine singular. From root k-w-n (to be, to exist). When used with divine attributes, kāna does not indicate past tense in the temporal sense but rather establishes an eternal, pre-existing quality. kāna + indefinite accusative predicate (tawwāban) is a Quranic formula for stating inherent divine attributes.

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form I, 3rd person feminine singular. The feminine tāʾ suffix (-at) agrees with the dual subject yadā (grammatically feminine). The geminated (doubled) bāʾ (tabb-) is the core of the root, signaling intensity — the doubling enacts the meaning of destruction phonetically. The verb is intransitive here (no direct object), declaring a state of ruin upon the subject.

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. The masculine form (tabba, without tāʾ suffix) implies a masculine subject — the man himself (Abū Lahab), as opposed to the feminine tabbat which agrees with yadā. The subject is implied (mustatir/hidden pronoun huwa). This is the same root as word 1, creating a deliberate verbal repetition.

Form IV (أَفْعَلَ / afʿala) past tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular. Root غ ن ي (gh-n-y). Form IV adds causative meaning: "to cause someone to be ghanī (rich/self-sufficient)." MIXED transitivity (bundle: 9 with object, 7 without) — in this ayah, no explicit direct object, allowing intransitive reading: "did not become self-sufficient" alongside transitive "did not make [him] self-sufficient." The verb is fronted before its subject (māluhu), creating VSO order that foregrounds the FAILURE.
notes: the availing target is expressed by عَنْهُ

grammar: Form I (فَعَلَ / faʿala) past tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular. Root ك س ب (k-s-b). MIXED transitivity (bundle: 33 with object, 10 without) — in this ayah, no explicit object appears. The elided object is replaced by the relative pronoun mā ("what"), making the construction "what he earned" — the earning is acknowledged but its specifics deliberately withheld. The subject (he = Abū Lahab) is implied from context.

Imperfect verb, read as Form IV (yuṣlā) with sa- prefix for definite future. 3rd person masculine singular. Form IV (aṣlā / yuṣlā) is causative: "to cause someone to enter/endure fire." The implicit subject is "he" (Abu Lahab, from 111:1). The sa- prefix marks certainty of future occurrence — stronger than sawfa.

Form I imperative (fi'l amr), 2nd person masculine singular, jussive (majzum). The base form is qāla/yaqūlu; the imperative qul drops the weak middle radical. Addresses Muhammad directly as the commanded speaker.

Imperfect (muḍāriʿ) verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular, jussive mood (majzūm) after lam. From weak-initial w-l-d with initial wāw dropped in the imperfect (walada → yalidu). Active voice: the subject (God) is the agent of begetting.

Imperfect (muḍāriʿ) verb, Form I, 3rd person masculine singular, passive voice (majhūl), jussive mood (majzūm) after lam. Root w-l-d. The passive transforms the subject from agent to patient: God is denied as the product of any generative process. The jussive apocopates: yūladu → yūlad.

Apocopated imperfect verb (muzari majzum), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. Copular verb (kana/yakunu) negated by lam. The apocopation (loss of final -u) is caused by the jazm particle lam. Functions as incomplete/copular verb (fi'l naqis) requiring predicate.
notes: كُفُوًا is the kana predicate

grammar: Form I imperative (CV), 2nd person masculine singular, apocopated (majzūm). The base form is qāla/yaqūlu; the imperative qul drops the weak middle radical (hollow verb — wāw). Directed at the Prophet Muhammad as the addressee.

Form I imperfect (muḍāri'), 1st person singular. Root '-w-dh. The imperfect tense indicates ongoing, continuous, or habitual action — not a one-time request but a perpetual state of seeking refuge. No explicit direct object in this ayah.

Perfect verb (fi'l māḍī), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular; subject (fā'il) is elided — understood as God (Allāh) from context of 113:1 (qul a'ūdhu bi-rabbi l-falaq); the verb is absolute (no explicit object), with mā functioning as the antecedent

Perfect verb (fi'l māḍī), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. Intransitive (no direct object). The subject is the implied ghāsiq — the darkening one. waqaba is a hapax legomenon in the Quran (occurs only in this ayah). The perfect tense in an idhā clause creates iterative meaning: "whenever it penetrates." The verb has no explicit object, making the penetration absolute and directionless — it penetrates EVERYTHING, not a specific target.

Perfect verb (fiʿl māḍī), Form I, 3rd person masculine singular. Used with إِذَا to express habitual/future conditionality. Intransitive here — no explicit direct object stated. The verb's root echoes the preceding active participle حَاسِدٍ, creating a cognate accusative-like structure (ḥāsid... ḥasada).
notes: no explicit envied object

grammar: Imperative verb (fiʿl amr), second person masculine singular, from root q-l-l (Form I: qāla/yaqūlu). The apocopated form qul (with sukūn on lām) is the standard imperative. Addressed to the Prophet Muhammad, but applicable to any reader — the command frames all subsequent speech as divinely instructed, not spontaneous.

Imperfect verb (fiʿl muḍāriʿ), first person singular, Form I (faʿala/yafʿulu pattern: ʿādha/yaʿūdhu). The imperfect tense indicates ongoing, habitual, or renewed action — not a one-time act but a continuous state of seeking refuge. No explicit direct object in this ayah; the source of refuge is marked by bi- (bi-rabbi).

Imperfect verb, Form I (quadriliteral/reduplicated), 3rd person masculine singular. The imperfect indicates ongoing, habitual action. The reduplicated root mirrors the repetitive nature of the action. Subject is the implied referent of alladhi (al-waswas). Transitivity: MIXED — here used WITHOUT explicit object (intransitive reading).
